title: Daniel 2:31–45
context: Daniel tells the forgotten dream: a great image of gold, silver, bronze, iron, and mixed feet, struck by a stone cut without hands. The image becomes chaff; the stone becomes a mountain filling the earth. Interpretation: Nebuchadnezzar is the head of gold; three kingdoms follow; in their days the God of heaven sets up a kingdom which will never be destroyed. Historic Christian reading: the stone is Christ’s kingdom.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What older interpreters in each camp said about four kingdoms and a stone cut without hands that becomes a mountain, agreed that the stone is Christ’s kingdom.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: In the days of these kings—while the iron kingdom stood, for Christ was born in the reign of Augustus Caesar. And this kingdom is not bounded by any limits, as worldly empires are, but is truly universal. And it shall be for ever, never destroyed or given to others, as the rest were. And the gold—this denotes the small beginning of Christ’s visible kingdom, and the different rise of Christ from all other; his conception by the Holy Ghost, without father and mother, respectively as to his two natures. This stone, falling from the mountain, brake the image in pieces; for Christ is a stone that grinds to powder those it falls on: and he is a growing stone even to a mountain, and therefore will fill the earth.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Dan 2:44–45)

reformed.quote: God wished, under this figure, to represent the future condition of the world till the advent of Christ. Earthly empires are swallowed and broken up by Christ accidentally, as they say. If kings exercise their office honestly, Christ’s kingdom is not contrary to their power. Whence then does it happen that Christ strikes kings with an iron scepter? Because their pride is untamable. Before Christ appeared, he already possessed supreme power, both in heaven and earth, and thus broke up and annihilated the pride and violence of all men. The stone was cut out of the mountain without hands, because the origin of Christ’s kingdom is not human.

verses.text: “You, O king, saw, and behold, a great image. This image, which was mighty, and whose brightness was excellent, stood before you; and its appearance was terrifying.
verses.arminianNotes:
A great image, mighty, bright, frightening. Wesley will read four monarchies and then Christ’s kingdom. The terror is the king’s, not a cue for a culture-war on empire.

The vision reveals the kingdoms to come. The Most High who changes times (2:21) now shows their shape. Human empires stand and frighten; they are still creatures under the stone that is coming.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: not with natural eyes; a specimen of revelation. Interpreters of moderate judgment explain it of four monarchies—Babylonian, Persian, Macedonian, Roman. God does not regard agreement among them, but the state of the world till Christ. One image because one world-course, not because the empires were one soul.

The fright is God’s sting still working. Both traditions agree: a frightening image. The metals will be named; the stone will.

verses.text: As for this image, its head was of fine gold, its chest and its arms of silver, its belly and its thighs of bronze,
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: he was the head of gold because of vast riches, long standing, fortunate to the last. Inferior kingdoms follow in time and peace, not a slogan about “civilization.”

The realms follow one another, and each is only a creature. Gold is first, not final. The God of heaven gave the head (v. 37); the rest will arise by the same rule, with armies and years.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: gold by comparison, because the world grows worse as it ages. We must not look at one man’s character (Cyrus’s valor) but the continued state of the empire. Experience shows degeneration. Shared names: Babylon, then Medes and Persians, then Greece.

The decline is inside providence, not luck. Wesley agrees: gold, silver, bronze as those three. Rome waits in the iron.

verses.text: its legs of iron, its feet part of iron and part of clay.
verses.arminianNotes:
Legs iron; feet iron and clay. Wesley: the Roman kingdom, strong as iron, later divided, partly strong and partly weak. Division is history, not a modern map to fight over.

“Feet”—a mixture. Strength and brittleness together under the Most High. Human politics mix and fail; the stone will not need them to hold.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: iron fits Roman cruelty, ambition, avarice— on “Rome” as a present cause. Clay in the feet: the ruin when God dispersed that monarchy; it fell by itself according to this word, broken up by Christ.

Even the mix is foretold. The strike lands here (v. 34).

verses.text: You saw until a stone was cut out without hands, which struck the image on its feet that were of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces.
verses.arminianNotes:
A stone cut out by no human hand strikes the feet and breaks them. Wesley: different rise of Christ from all other; conception by the Holy Ghost; a stone that grinds to powder those it falls on.

Both camps confess this is Christ and His kingdom—not a rapture timetable. Cut without hands: the kingdom is God’s doing. It still meets feet: Rome’s mix, history.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: why Christ breaks the image if by Him kings reign—empires are broken accidentally, when pride will not bow. If kings exercise office honestly, Christ’s kingdom is not contrary to their power. Untamable pride feels the iron scepter. Cut without hands: origin not human.

“Stone”—already the eternal wisdom, already supreme before the open advent. Shared christology: the stone is Christ.

verses.text: Then the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver, and the gold were broken in pieces together, and became like the chaff of the summer threshing floors. The wind carried them away, so that no place was found for them. The stone that struck the image became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.
verses.arminianNotes:
All metals chaff; wind carries them; no trace; the stone becomes a mountain filling the earth. Wesley: a growing stone even to a mountain, and therefore will fill the earth. Small beginning of Christ’s visible kingdom.

Growth that fills. The gospel sincerely runs; nations may receive or grind.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the image perishes as Christ takes what was splendid. The fashion of this world passes; this vision marks the four until renovation in Christ. The mountain is the kingdom, not a human pile.

Effectual filling, not a bare offer that may leave the earth empty. On this both agree: chaff for the metals, a mountain for the stone. Both mean Christ’s kingdom, forever (v. 44).

verses.text: “This is the dream; and we will tell its interpretation before the king.
verses.arminianNotes:
This was the dream; we will tell the interpretation. Wesley: by this word “we” appears Daniel’s piety and modesty, or he declares that he and his companions had begged this skill from God, and therefore he did not arrogate it to himself.

“We”—the prayers of 2:18 still sit in the room. Gift shared, not a solo genius. Interpretation is mercy for a king, not a weapon.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he now records the dream and will not touch interpretation without the matter itself. What follows confirms the four monarchies and the stone.

Even the modest plural is inside the revelation already given. Shared: dream first, then meaning. The God of heaven is about to be named as Giver.

verses.text: You, O king, are king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given the kingdom, the power, the strength, and the glory.
verses.arminianNotes:
King of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given the kingdom, the power, the strength, and the glory. Wesley: He hath given thee absolute dominion of all creatures within the bounds of thy vast kingdom. The giving here matches 2:21.

Nebuchadnezzar’s power is a gift from the God of heaven, which makes him answerable for how he uses it—including the death decree of 2:12. Arminians read “king of kings” as a title held under a higher King.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the God of heaven has given—not valor, counsel, fortune, or luck, as 1:2 already taught. He appoints kings and raises them from the rest of mankind as He pleases. Government remains with the one God.

“Given”—effectual appointment, not a bare permission after Babylon rose. The power, might, and glory are His loan. Nothing happens but what He has knowingly and willingly decreed, yet He is not the author of the king’s fury as fury.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess the Most High rules: the God of heaven has given the kingdom (2:37), as He changes times and kings (2:21). Arminians hear imperial agency under that gift. Reformed Christians hear effectual appointment, not a bare permission (Calvin).

verses.text: Wherever the children of men dwell, he has given the animals of the field and the birds of the sky into your hand, and has made you rule over them all. You are the head of gold.
verses.arminianNotes:
Into his hand: mankind, beasts, birds; he is the head of gold. Wesley: first in order, as the head is before the other parts; the vision began in him and descended; gold for riches, length, and flourishing.

A named man, a named gift. Dominion over creatures is Genesis language under exile.” The head is gold and mortal.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: wherever they dwell—the grant is wide and still a grant. Gold names the first monarchy, not a metal to hoard as theology.

The hand that holds beasts is the hand God filled. Shared with Wesley: you are the head of gold. Inferior kingdoms will not make this untrue; they will make it second.

verses.text: “After you, another kingdom will arise that is inferior to you; and another third kingdom of bronze, which will rule over all the earth.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Medes and Persians, inferior in time, not half so long in prosperity, yet rich and large; third the Grecian under Alexander, coarser, marching even to the Indies, said to conquer the world.

The second and third kingdoms are named. Inferior does not mean unreal. The God who removes kings (2:21) does it through Medes, Persians, and Greeks who actually fight.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: Medes and Persians worse in morals than the first; Macedonian bronze for Alexander’s cruelty and his successors’ blood, family exterminated. Do not restrict the third to one man’s politeness.

Each rise is appointment, each fall judgment. Shared names: Persia, then Greece. No invented fourth before Rome.

verses.text: The fourth kingdom will be strong as iron, because iron breaks in pieces and subdues all things; and as iron that crushes all these, it will break in pieces and crush.
verses.arminianNotes:
A fourth, strong as iron, breaking and crushing all. Wesley: the kingdom of the Romans, to last not only to Christ’s first coming, but under antichrist, to his second coming; it broke in pieces all other kingdoms till the stone fell upon it.

Rome, as Wesley and Calvin both read. Wesley extends that iron under antichrist toward the second coming; that is his note, not a modern rapture chart, and not the Arminian-versus-Reformed fork. Shared christology still waits on the stone (vv. 44–45).
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: iron for Roman tyranny; the world worse as it aged. The fourth is Rome until Christ openly breaks the image. He reads the advent as already the stone’s strike.

Rome’s crush is true and under decree. Fourth = Rome in the classic Christian reading.

verses.text: Whereas you saw the feet and toes, part of potters’ clay and part of iron, it will be a divided kingdom; but there will be in it of the strength of the iron, because you saw the iron mixed with miry clay.
verses.arminianNotes:
Feet and toes, clay and iron: a divided kingdom, some firmness remaining. Wesley: partly strong, partly weak; divided by civil wars and by provinces casting off the yoke, into ten kingdoms or toes.

The mixture reflects the course of history. Ten toes in Wesley are his reading of later fracture, not a license for date-setting or culture maps. Brittleness is still under the God who sets up kings.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: clay points to ruin without needing a chart of ten modern states. The monarchy mixed and did not last as gold had lasted.

Providence includes the mix. Iron and clay together. The stone hits the feet.

verses.text: As the toes of the feet were part of iron, and part of clay, so the kingdom will be partly strong and partly brittle.
verses.arminianNotes:
Toes partly iron, partly clay: partly strong, partly brittle. Wesley: plain in the civil wars of the Romans, and the falling off of some countries, especially toward the end.

The toes show weakness within an empire. Strong and weak together is not a parable about present parties.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the feet’s clay is why it could fall without a fifth metal. Christ is the cause the image does not stand.

“Brittle”—appointed fracture. Common ground: partly strong, partly brittle. Marriage-mix follows.

verses.text: Whereas you saw the iron mixed with miry clay, they will mingle themselves with the seed of men; but they won’t cling to one another, even as iron does not mix with clay.
verses.arminianNotes:
They mix in marriage but will not hold, as iron does not mix with clay. Wesley: by marriage, but they shall never knit well, because ambition is stronger than affinity.

Human schemes to glue a divided realm. Agency under rule—alliances are true and fail. Not a sermon on modern weddings or politics.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: they try to unite what God has shown will not cohere. Ambition and policy cannot reverse the vision.

Even the marriages sit inside the decree that they will not hold. Both traditions agree: iron does not mix with clay. The next verse is the kingdom that does hold.

verses.text: “In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom which will never be destroyed, nor will its sovereignty be left to another people; but it will break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it will stand forever.
verses.arminianNotes:
In the days of those kings the God of heaven sets up a kingdom never destroyed, not left to another people; but it breaks the others and stands forever. Wesley: while the iron kingdom stood, for Christ was born in the reign of Augustus. Not bounded as worldly empires; truly universal; for ever.

Both camps confess this is Christ’s. Set up in those kings’ days: the first advent, under Rome. The kingdom sincerely gathers; it is not a human handoff. Forever means forever.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: God of heaven sets it up—the same Giver as v. 37. Christ already possessed supreme power before He appeared; at the advent He overthrows these monarchies. If kings serve honestly, His kingdom is not contrary to their power; pride finds the scepter. It shall stand forever: not left to another people.

God’s kingdom is effectual, divine, and unending. Shared christology with Wesley: born under Rome, kingdom forever, breaks the image. Difference of accent on how far they trace Rome’s iron is.

verses.text: Because you saw that a stone was cut out of the mountain without hands, and that it broke in pieces the iron, the bronze, the clay, the silver, and the gold, the great God has made known to the king what will happen hereafter. The dream is certain, and its interpretation sure.”
verses.arminianNotes:
A stone cut out of the mountain without hands; it broke the metals. The great God has made known what shall be; the dream is certain, the interpretation sure. Wesley: small beginning of Christ’s visible kingdom; conception by the Holy Ghost as to His two natures; a stone that grinds to powder; a growing stone to a mountain filling the earth.

Certain because God spoke, not because Daniel was clever (2:30). The stone is Christ; filling the earth is the gospel’s reach. Hearers remain responsible under that sure word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: cut without hands—the origin of Christ’s kingdom is not human. The great God has made it known: the same God who reveals secrets (2:28). Certain and sure, so the king cannot treat it as a Magi’s guess.

The interpretation stands because God decreed the history it names. Shared with Wesley: no human hand, Christ’s kingdom, the earth filled. The next range is the king’s homage.
